description_full: CMOC Group Limited, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the mining, beneficiation, and smelting of base and rare metals in Asia, Africa, South America, and Europe. It operates through Molybdenum and Tungsten Related Products; Niobium and Phosphorus Related Products; Copper-Cobalt Related Products; Mineral and Metal Trade; Refined Metals Trade; and Others segments. The company offers copper, gold, cobalt, molybdenum, tungsten, and niobium; and phosphate fertilizer. It also engages in trading in base metals, and molybdenum and tungstenic products; selection, processing, refining, and sale of mineral products; import and export of goods and technology; consulting; asset and investment management; enterprise operation and management; technology services; logistics transportation; technical services and software development; and hotel operation activities. The company was formerly known as China Molybdenum Co., Ltd. and changed its name to CMOC Group Limited in June 2022. CMOC Group Limited was founded in 1969 and is based in Luoyang, the People's Republic of China.

financial_summary: CMOC GROUP LTD is a large-cap basic materials business with a $38.0B market cap on $31.0B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are expanding by +4.5pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at 20% against a 8% cost of capital — a 12-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 13% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The business throws off $2.0B in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 16× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 3.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Cyclical sectors like Basic Materials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.
